procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated July 19, 1965 of the Punjab High Court, Circuit Bench at Delhi in Regular Second Appeal No. 251-D of 1964.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Trial Court dismissed the suit. The first appellate court affirmed the decree of the Trial Court. The High Court affirmed the decree of the Trial Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Badri Pershad, the plaintiff in the original suit, appealed to the Supreme Court after losing in the Trial Court, the First Appellate Court, and the High Court. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.

directions: This appeal fails and it is dismissed with costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether the case of a Hindu female who acquires an interest in property under the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937, which is subsequently separated by a partition award, is governed by Section 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, thereby granting her only a restricted estate.

facts: A Hindu widow acquired an interest in her deceased husband's property under the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937.
Subsequently, an arbitrator was appointed to partition the property among the heirs.
The arbitrator's award, which was made into a court decree, allotted the widow her share but stated that she was to have a limited "widow's estate" in those properties.
law: Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, states that any property possessed by a female Hindu, whether acquired before or after the Act, shall be held by her as a full owner, not a limited owner. The explanation clarifies that "property" includes that which is acquired at a partition.

Section 14(2) of the Act is an exception to Section 14(1). It states that Section 14(1) will not apply to property acquired under an award (or will, gift, decree, etc.) where the terms of that instrument specifically prescribe a restricted estate.
application: The Court determined that the widow's right to the property was a "pre-existing right" that she acquired under the 1937 Act, not from the partition award.

The partition award did not create a new right for her for the first time; it only separated her pre-existing share by metes and bounds. Therefore, she "acquired" the property at a partition, which falls squarely under Section 14(1).

The Court reasoned that Section 14(2) acts as a proviso or exception and only applies when a female Hindu acquires property for the first time through an instrument like an award, without having any pre-existing right to it.
Since the widow already had an interest in the property before the award, her case is governed by the general rule in Section 14(1), not the exception in Section 14(2).

The fact that the award described her interest as a limited "widow's estate" was irrelevant because Section 14(1) automatically upgraded her pre-existing limited ownership to full ownership when the 1956 Act came into force.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the widow's property was governed by Section 14(2). It held that because her right to the property pre-existed the award (originating from the 1937 Act), Section 14(1) applied, making her the full owner of the property, notwithstanding the restrictive terms in the partition award.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the case of a Hindu female who acquires an interest in property under the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937, which is subsequently separated by a partition award, is governed by Section 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, thereby granting her only a restricted estate.
appellant_arguments: The respondent acquired the property under the award or the decree based on it, which are instruments that fall under Section 14(2).
The award explicitly stated that the respondent would have a "widow's estate," which is a restricted estate, thereby making Section 14(2) applicable and excluding Section 14(1).
In interpreting Section 14, a court should first examine if the case falls under the exception in sub-section (2), and only if it does not, should sub-section (1) be applied.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's right to the property was a pre-existing interest acquired under the Hindu Women's Right to Property Act, 1937.
The award did not create a new right; it merely separated her pre-existing share by metes and bounds in a partition.

The property was therefore acquired "at a partition" as per the Explanation to Section 14(1), and since she possessed it when the 1956 Act came into force, her limited ownership was enlarged to full ownership under Section 14(1).

statutes.act_name: Hindu Women's Right to Property Act, 1937 (Act XVIII of 1937)

cases.principle: Section 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act clarifies that the object of Section 14 was to remove the disability on women imposed by law and not to interfere with contracts, grants, or decrees by virtue of which a woman's right was restricted.

cases.case_name: Sukhram & Another v. Gauri Shankar & Another
cases.principle: A female Hindu who acquired an interest in joint family property under the Hindu Women's Right to Property Act, 1937, becomes a full owner of that property by virtue of Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Section 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act is an exception to Section 14(1) and applies only when a female Hindu acquires a property for the first time through an instrument (such as a gift, will, decree, or award) that prescribes a restricted estate, where she had no pre-existing right to the property. If a female Hindu already has a pre-existing right in a property, an instrument that merely separates or allots her share does not fall under Section 14(2); instead, her right is enlarged to full ownership under Section 14(1).

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Section 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, operates as a proviso or exception to Section 14(1) and applies only when a property is acquired by a female Hindu for the first time under an instrument, like an award or decree, that prescribes a restricted estate. It does not apply where the female Hindu has a pre-existing right to the property, such as an interest acquired under the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937. In such cases, a subsequent partition award that separates her share by metes and bounds does not create a new right but merely formalizes the pre-existing one, bringing the case under Section 14(1) and enlarging her limited estate into full ownership.
legal_tests_applied: Section 14(2) can come into operation only if acquisition in any of the methods indicated therein is made for the first time without there being any pre-existing right in the female Hindu who is in possession of the property.
Section 14(2) is to be interpreted as a proviso or an exception to Section 14(1), and the section must be read as a whole, not by first examining the exception in sub-section (2).
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that a court should first look at sub-section (2) before considering sub-section (1) was rejected as a manner of reading the section that is 'not warranted either on principle or authority.'

The partition award did not create a new right in the respondent for the first time; it merely separated a share in property to which she already had a pre-existing right under the 1937 Act. Therefore, the award did not bring the matter within the scope of Section 14(2).

The mere fact that the partition resulted in an award and a decree based on it was insufficient to trigger Section 14(2), as the provisions of Section 14(1) were fully applicable, especially in view of the express terms of its Explanation which includes property acquired 'at a partition'.
why_respondent_won: The respondent had a pre-existing right to the property, having acquired an interest under the Hindu Women's Right to Property Act, 1937, upon her husband's death.

The award did not grant her property for the first time; it simply separated her pre-existing share by metes and bounds, which constitutes an acquisition 'at a partition' as specified in the Explanation to Section 14(1).

Because the respondent had a pre-existing right and was in possession of the property acquired at a partition when the 1956 Act came into force, her case was governed by Section 14(1), which enlarged her limited estate into that of a full owner.
policy_considerations: The object of Section 14 was only to remove the disability on women imposed by law and not to interfere with contracts, grants or decrees etc. by virtue of which a woman's right was restricted.
